steps.reasoning: Treat as given the effective four‑component Hamiltonian and the empirical existence of magic configurations (conclusions 1 and 2): take the Hamiltonian parametrized by $(U,V,K_M,v,\omega_0)$ and the previously identified magic distances (where $\Delta\omega\approx0$) as known starting points for the tight‑binding and localization analysis.

Motivate a single‑band tight‐binding picture from Fourier decomposition of the band: note that an energy band $E(q)$ in the moiré Brillouin zone (with moiré wavevector half‑width $q_0=K_M/2$) is an even periodic function and can be expanded in cosine Fourier components $f_p=\frac{1}{2q_0}\int_{-q_0}^{+q_0}\mathrm{d}q\,\cos\big(p\pi/q_0\big)E(q)$; numerically compute these Fourier coefficients for the moiré miniband and observe that the first Fourier harmonic ($p=1$) dominates over higher harmonics for the parameter ranges studied, indicating that the band dispersion is well approximated by a single cosine, which in real‑space corresponds to a nearest‑neighbour tight‑binding model with dominant nearest‑neighbour tunnelling. This observation is supported by the plotted Fourier components (supplemental figure) showing first‑component dominance. 
Fig. S5

Define the single‑band tight‑binding model and identify the tunnelling amplitude: introduce a single‑band tight‑binding Hamiltonian with Wannier orbitals $W_0(x)$ localized at moiré lattice sites and nearest‑neighbour tunnelling amplitude $J$ (a scalar), so that the tight‑binding dispersion for the isolated miniband is $\omega(q)=\omega_{\text{loc}}+2J\cos(qa)$ in the simplest nearest‑neighbour truncation where $a$ is the moiré period and $\omega_{\text{loc}}$ is the on‑site energy; therefore the miniband bandwidth is $2|J|$ if the first Fourier component dominates, establishing the quantitative relation between $J$ and the miniband global spectral bandwidth.

Compute maximally localized Wannier functions and quantify localization: using the twisted parallel‑transport gauge (the constructive one‑dimensional gauge fixing procedure for maximally localized Wannier functions), compute the Wannier function
$$
W_0(x)=\frac{1}{2q_0}\int_{-q_0}^{+q_0}\mathrm{d}q\;e^{iqx}u_q(x),
$$
where $u_q(x)$ is the periodic four‑spinor Bloch eigenfunction of the moiré Hamiltonian and $q_0=K_M/2$; numerically evaluate the probability density $|W_0(x)|^2$ for the hole‑like miniband and find that more than $94\%$ of the Wannier density is located within a single moiré period for the parameter ranges studied, confirming that $W_0(x)$ is tightly localized and thus suitable as a single‑orbital basis for a nearest‑neighbour tight‑binding model. This computation is reported in the paper and visualized in Fig.4(a) and Fig. S7. 
Fig. 4(a)
Fig. S7

Connect flatband formation to vanishing nearest‑neighbour tunnelling: combine the empirical fact that the miniband bandwidth is dominated by the first Fourier harmonic (so bandwidth $\approx 2|J|$) with the observation that at magic distances $\Delta\omega\to 0$; conclude that the flatband occurs when the effective nearest‑neighbour tunnelling amplitude $J$ vanishes (i.e., $J=0$ gives a dispersionless band when only the first harmonic is significant). Note that the authors also caution that higher Fourier components do not vanish at the same point, which is why bands become almost‑flat rather than perfectly flat. 
Fig. S5

Demonstrate the sign change and zero‑crossing of $J$ via a finite "diatomic moiré molecule": construct a finite system composed of two moiré cells (a "diatomic moiré molecule"), compute its two bound states (even and odd parity) analytically via the transfer‑matrix method for the effective Hamiltonian and numerically via Finite‑Difference Time‑Domain (FDTD) simulations, and track the energy splitting $\Delta E$ between the even and odd bound states as a function of inter‑layer spacing $L$ (which controls $V$ and hence $V/U$); find that $\Delta E$ crosses zero exactly at the magic distances identified in the infinite periodic system, which implies that the effective two‑site tunnelling amplitude $J$ changes sign and vanishes at the same parameter values. This comparison is shown by the matching analytical and FDTD results in Fig.4(c–e). 
Fig. 4b-e
[25,26]

Conclude the correspondence between bound‑state degeneracy and flatband localization: interpret the diatomic molecule degeneracy at the magic distances as the finite‑system signature of $J\to 0$, and combine this with the Wannier localization result to conclude that flatband formation corresponds to vanishing nearest‑neighbour tunnelling and to tightly localized photonic Wannier orbitals concentrated within a single moiré cell; therefore each isolated moiré miniband admits a single‑band tight‑binding description in terms of maximally localized Wannier orbitals $W_0(x)$ and an effective nearest‑neighbour tunnelling amplitude $J$ that can be tuned (and set to zero) by varying inter‑layer coupling $V$ (via $L$) and intra‑layer coupling $U$ (via $\kappa$). 
Fig. 4a

Record limitations and explicit numerical confirmations: note that the Wannier functions, while highly localized, still have finite tails beyond a moiré cell and that higher Fourier components remain nonzero at the magic coupling, so the bands are almost‑flat rather than perfectly flat; nevertheless, numerical RCWA, Hamiltonian, and FDTD/transfer‑matrix comparisons consistently confirm the interpretation that $J\to0$ at magic distances and that the associated photonic states are tightly localized within a moiré period. 
Fig. S6

motivating_questions.content: For photonic device engineering and for mapping to many‑body or nonlinear lattice physics, it is essential to know whether moiré minibands admit a compact lattice description (single orbital per moiré cell) with a well‑defined tunnelling parameter that can be tuned by geometry. Prior to this work, there was no demonstration that (a) Wannier orbitals in bilayer photonic moiré can be computed with high localization; (b) the miniband dispersion is dominated by the nearest‑neighbour hopping (so that a textbook single‑band tight‑binding model applies); and (c) the hopping amplitude can be driven continuously through zero via inter-layer spacing, thereby enabling localization at a single moiré site. Without such mapping one cannot reduce full-wave electromagnetic results to a lattice Hamiltonian amenable to many‑body or nonlinear analyses, nor design resonator arrays with controlled coupling strength or sign.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: Numerical solutions of the strained continuum model demonstrate that applied strain (uniaxial heterostrain, shear, or biaxial) tends to prevent the formation of the narrow/flat moiré bands known from unstrained magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. Even when strain-only configurations produce hexagonal moiré periodicities identical in length to a twist-only moiré, the lowest moiré bands do not flatten; instead strain reorganizes the band dispersion, shifts the Dirac points, splits van Hove singularities, and produces multiple higher-order van Hove peaks in the density of states, and modifies the real-space moiré charge-density profile.

The claim that strain suppresses moiré flat bands and that no new flat-band conditions exist under strain is based on numerical solutions of the continuum model for a limited set of strain parameters: uniaxial heterostrain at twist angle $\theta=1.05^\circ$ with two strain values (approximately $\epsilon=0.4\%$ and $\epsilon=0.8\%$ at specific angles $\phi$, producing moiré angles $\beta=105^\circ$ and $90^\circ$), and pure shear strain with $\epsilon_s=1.83\%$ and biaxial strain with $\epsilon_b=1.83\%$ (producing moiré periodicity equivalent to $\theta=1.05^\circ$). The paper does not perform a systematic scan over twist angles, strain magnitudes, or strain directions to rule out the existence of flat bands at other parameter combinations. The claim that strain 'does not shift the magic angle to a new value, or leads to new flat bands conditions' is a strong negative claim that is not supported by exhaustive numerical evidence.

premises.content:
For a valley index $\zeta$ (with $\zeta=+1$ for the $K$ valley and $\zeta=-1$ for the $K'$ valley), the low-energy continuum model Hamiltonian for a strained twisted bilayer graphene system under small strain and small twist angle $\theta$ is
      $$
      H_{\zeta}=\begin{pmatrix}
      h_{-,\zeta}(\mathbf{q})-\mathbb{I}V & U^\dagger(\mathbf{r})\\
      U(\mathbf{r}) & h_{+,\zeta}(\mathbf{q})+\mathbb{I}V
      \end{pmatrix},
      $$
      where $\mathbf{q}$ is momentum measured from the Dirac point, $\mathbb{I}$ the $2\times2$ identity, and $V$ the scalar deformation potential. The layer Dirac Hamiltonians are
      $$
      h_{\ell,\zeta}(\mathbf{q})=-\hbar v_F\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_\zeta\cdot\mathrm{R}^\mathrm{T}(\ell\tfrac{\theta}{2})(1+\tfrac{\ell\mathcal{E}}{2})(\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{D}_{\ell,\zeta}),
      $$
      with $v_F$ the Fermi velocity, $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_\zeta=(\zeta\sigma_x,\sigma_y)$ ($\sigma_i$ Pauli matrices), $\mathrm{R}(\phi)$ the $2\times2$ rotation matrix by angle $\phi$, $\ell=+$ for top layer and $\ell=-$ for bottom layer, $\mathcal{E}$ the strain tensor applied oppositely ($\mathcal{E}_+ = -\mathcal{E}_- = \mathcal{E}/2$), and $\mathbf{D}_{\ell,\zeta}$ the shifted Dirac points. The shifted Dirac points are
      $$
      \mathbf{D}_{\ell,\zeta}\simeq(\mathbb{I}-\tfrac{\ell\mathcal{E}}{2})\mathrm{R}(\ell\tfrac{\theta}{2})\mathbf{K}_\zeta-\ell\zeta\mathbf{A},
      $$
      where $\mathbf{K}_\zeta = -\zeta(2\mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2)/3$ is the Dirac point in the undeformed honeycomb lattice (with $\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2$ the honeycomb reciprocal vectors), and $\mathbf{A}$ is the strain-induced pseudo-gauge field. The pseudo-gauge field is
      $$
      \mathbf{A}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2a}\beta_G(\epsilon_{xx}-\epsilon_{yy},-2\epsilon_{xy}),
      $$
      with $a\approx 2.46$ Å the lattice constant, $\beta_G\approx 3.14$ the Grüneisen parameter, and $\epsilon_{ij}$ components of $\mathcal{E}$. The scalar deformation potential is $V=g(\epsilon_{xx}+\epsilon_{yy})$, with $g=4$ eV. The interlayer moiré coupling matrix $U(\mathbf{r})$ admits a rapidly converging Fourier expansion; to leading order it reduces to three terms
      $$
      U(\mathbf{r})\simeq U_0+U_1 e^{i\zeta\mathbf{g}_1\cdot\mathbf{r}}+U_1^\mathrm{T}e^{i\zeta(\mathbf{g}_1+\mathbf{g}_2)\cdot\mathbf{r}},
      $$
      where $\mathbf{g}_i$ are the moiré reciprocal vectors (given by $\mathbf{g}_i=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{b}_i$ with $\mathbf{T}=(\mathbb{I}+\mathcal{E}/2)\mathrm{R}(-\theta/2)-(\mathbb{I}-\mathcal{E}/2)\mathrm{R}(\theta/2)$). The coupling matrices are $U_0 = \begin{pmatrix} u_0 & u_1 \\ u_1 & u_0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $U_1 = \begin{pmatrix} u_0 & u_1 \omega^{-\zeta\xi} \\ u_1 \omega^{\zeta\xi} & u_0 \end{pmatrix}$, with $\omega=e^{i2\pi/3}$, $u_0$ and $u_1=90$ meV the $AA$ and $AB$ hopping energies, and $\xi=\pm1$ a strain-dependent phase factor encoding the relative phases of the three momentum transfers. This extension explicitly incorporates the effects of arbitrary small strain (through $\mathcal{E}$, $\mathbf{A}$, $V$, and modified $\mathbf{g}_i$) into standard moiré continuum modeling.

steps.reasoning: Take as established the strained continuum model Hamiltonian and its ingredients from conclusion 10 (shifted Dirac points $\mathbf{D}_{\ell,\zeta}$, pseudo-gauge $\mathbf{A}$, scalar potential $V$, and interlayer coupling $U(\mathbf{r})$ with strained $\mathbf{g}_i$); use this model as the starting point for numerical diagonalization to obtain band structures and densities of states (DOS) for given twist and strain parameters.

Explain the numerical strategy (as used by the authors): truncate the Fourier expansion of $U(\mathbf{r})$ at the leading three momentum transfers (authors justify this because hopping amplitudes decay rapidly with momentum, $t(2K)\ll t(K)$), represent the Hamiltonian in a plane-wave / moiré-BZ basis built from the primitive mBZ corners (conclusion 9), and numerically diagonalize for representative parameter sets (e.g., magic-angle twist $\theta\approx1.05^\circ$ with small uniaxial heterostrain, and pure-strain hexagonal cases matched to that moiré periodicity).
[77]

Describe the numerical observations for heterostrain plus twist (authors' Fig. 8): for $\theta=1.05^\circ$ and small uniaxial heterostrain values ($\epsilon\simeq0.4\%$ and $\epsilon\simeq0.8\%$ with respective angles $\phi$ producing moiré angles $\beta=105^\circ$ and $90^\circ$), the computed band structures show that the extremely narrow/flat moiré bands present in the unstrained magic-angle case are no longer formed; instead the low-energy bands are broadened, Dirac points are shifted away from high-symmetry mBZ corners, and the band dispersion reorganizes, as illustrated by the authors' 3D band and DOS plots.
Fig. 8

Present the authors' momentum-shift explanation using the difference between shifted Dirac points: the vector difference between shifted Dirac points in the two layers is
$$
\Delta\mathbf{D}=\mathbf{D}_--\mathbf{D}_+\;=\;-\frac{2\mathbf{g}_1+\mathbf{g}_2}{3}+2\mathbf{A},
$$
where $\mathbf{g}_i$ are the strained moiré vectors and $\mathbf{A}$ is the pseudo-gauge; because $\mathbf{A}\neq0$ under strain (or because $\beta\neq120^\circ$), $\Delta\mathbf{D}$ in general does not coincide with the primitive mBZ corner $\mathbf{Q}_1$, meaning the Dirac cones are displaced relative to the mBZ and thus coupled differently by the moiré potential, which alters the low-energy band structure.

Report the authors' comparison of hexagonal moiré patterns produced by (i) twist-only, (ii) shear-only, and (iii) biaxial-only strain but tuned to the same moiré periodicity (via $\epsilon_s=2\sin(\tfrac{\theta}{2})$ and $\epsilon_b=2\sin(\tfrac{\theta}{2})$): numerically, only the twist-only case exhibits the characteristic flat bands (and concomitant strong peak in DOS); both shear-only and biaxial-only hexagonal moirés with the same period do not exhibit flattened lowest moiré bands, instead showing reorganized dispersions and multiple split and higher-order van Hove singularities in the DOS, as well as altered real-space moiré charge-density profiles.
Fig. 10

Note the robustness of the band-flattening suppression to removal of strain gauge and scalar potentials: the authors show in Appendix D that even setting $\mathbf{A}=0$ and $V=0$ (i.e., removing strain-induced gauge and scalar fields) does not restore flat bands — the continuum-model bands are still distorted by the strained moiré geometry and modified momentum transfers — indicating that the dominant mechanism for suppression is the change in the moiré coupling geometry (the relative orientations and magnitudes of the three momentum-transfer vectors $\mathbf{q}_i$) rather than only the local pseudo-gauge or scalar energy shifts.
Fig. 13

Conclude that, based on the numerical diagonalization of the strained continuum Hamiltonian across the representative parameter regimes, applied strain (uniaxial heterostrain, shear, or biaxial) tends to prevent the formation of the narrow/flat moiré bands known from unstrained magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, and instead reorganizes the band dispersion, shifts Dirac points, splits van Hove singularities producing multiple higher-order van Hove peaks in the DOS, and modifies the real-space moiré charge-density profile; these numerical findings establish the authors' electronic-structure conclusion.

motivating_questions.content: The experimental sensitivity of correlated phenomena to sample strain motivated a quantitative assessment of how strain affects the occurrence of flat bands. Previously, it was not established whether flat-band conditions (magic angles) merely shift under strain or are qualitatively destroyed. Without explicit continuum-model calculations including Dirac shifts, gauge and scalar terms, and the strained moiré coupling, one cannot determine whether small strains preserve, shift, or suppress flat bands, nor predict the concomitant changes in density of states and charge localization.
